turns.response_html:
To reliably detect when an AI agent running inside an Alacritty tmux pane has finished its task—so a manager script or orchestrator agent can take over—you need to cross the boundary between visual terminal output and programmatic state.

While the instinct is often to scrape the terminal screen for text, there are three distinct architectural patterns for this, ranging from native terminal hooks to robust inter-process communication (IPC).

Architecture Comparison

MethodReliabilityComplexityBest Used When...
1. File-System SignalingHighestLowYou can instruct the agent to output a marker file or JSON state when done.
2. Tmux Silence / PID PollingModerateVery LowYou want zero modifications to the agent or prompt; relies on process inactivity.
3. Pane Scraping (capture-pane)Low-ModerateMediumThe agent outputs specific, predictable text markers (like [ROADMAP_COMPLETE]) that you must catch from stdout.

Method 1: File-System Signaling (The Robust IPC Approach)

If you are already driving the agent via structured prompts and roadmaps, the cleanest approach is to decouple detection from the terminal entirely. Text scrolling in a terminal is ephemeral and prone to formatting glitches; the filesystem is deterministic.

Add a directive to the agent's system instructions or roadmap template:

"When you finish a milestone, write {"status": "milestone_done", "timestamp": <time>} to .agent_state.json. When the entire roadmap and retrospective are complete, write {"status": "project_complete"}."

Your manager agent or background script simply watches this file instead of monitoring tmux:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Manager loop watching for agent completion

STATE_FILE=".agent_state.json"

while true; do
  if [[ -f "$STATE_FILE" ]]; do
    STATUS=$(jq -r '.status' "$STATE_FILE" 2>/dev/null)
    
    if [[ "$STATUS" == "project_complete" ]]; do
      echo "Agent finished roadmap. Triggering retrospective processing..."
      # Run your state capture, git commit, or branch reset logic here
      rm -f "$STATE_FILE"
      break
    elif [[ "$STATUS" == "milestone_done" ]]; do
      echo "Milestone reached. Sending encouragement..."
      tmux send-keys -t my_session:0.0 "good job, please continue" C-m
      rm -f "$STATE_FILE"
    fi
  fi
  sleep 2
done

Method 2: Tmux Native Silence & Process Polling

If you want the terminal itself to tell you when the agent has gone idle (waiting for your "good job" prompt or finished entirely) without modifying the agent's prompt, leverage tmux's built-in monitor-silence or inspect the pane's process tree.

The monitor-silence Hook

Tmux can fire an internal event when a pane stops producing output for a set number of seconds:

# 1. Enable silence monitoring on the target pane (e.g., 5 seconds of no output)
tmux set-window-option -t my_session:0 monitor-silence 5

# 2. Bind a hook to execute your manager script when silence is detected
tmux set-hook -g alert-silence 'run-shell "/path/to/manager_trigger.sh #{pane_id}"'

Process State Polling

When an agent is actively generating code or running tools, its child process is consuming CPU. When it finishes and drops back to an interactive prompt, the process sleeps. You can poll the pane's active PID:

# Get the PID of the shell in the target pane
PANE_PID=$(tmux list-panes -t my_session:0 -F "#{pane_pid}")

# Check if child processes (node, python, codex, etc.) are actively running under that shell
ACTIVE_CHILDREN=$(pgrep -P "$PANE_PID" | wc -l)

if [ "$ACTIVE_CHILDREN" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "Pane is idle. Shell is waiting for input."
fi

Method 3: Programmatic Pane Scraping (capture-pane)

If you must inspect the actual text inside the tmux pane to know what just finished (e.g., distinguishing between a standard milestone pause and the final tooling retrospective), use tmux capture-pane.

Instead of piping visual text manually, your script can grab the last N lines of the pane's scrollback buffer silently:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

TARGET_PANE="my_session:0.0"

while true; do
  # Capture the last 20 lines of the pane, stripping ANSI color codes (-p prints to stdout)
  OUTPUT=$(tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -20)

  # Check for specific completion markers
  if echo "$OUTPUT" | grep -q "TOOLING-RETROSPECTIVE-COMPLETE"; then
    echo "Retrospective detected. Encapsulating state..."
    # Capture the entire buffer to a log file before resetting
    tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -1000 > "./retrospective_output.log"
    break
  elif echo "$OUTPUT" | grep -E -q "(Milestone [0-9]+ complete|Waiting for input)"; then
    echo "Agent paused at milestone."
  fi

  sleep 3
done

A Note on the "Fresh Branch" Strategy

Wiping the working branch and restarting from scratch after the roadmap completes is actually a brilliant way to prevent context collapse and bloat—it acts like clean-room refactoring.

To solve the modularity problem (keeping the good pieces without keeping the bloat), use the File-System Signaling method above to have the agent export an artifacts/ directory or a manifest.json at the end of the run. This manifest explicitly lists the decoupled modules, standalone utility scripts, or schema files that should survive the branch reset. Your manager script can stash or copy those specific files out of the workspace before you blow the branch away, transplanting only the clean, modular components into the new starting state.

This is a rock-solid, event-driven architecture. Using the filesystem as your primary trigger eliminates CPU-wasting polling loops entirely, and reserving terminal buffer scraping strictly for a "settling gate" is the exact right division of labor.

By capturing latest_agent_output.txt and committing it with each step, you are effectively attaching an immutable diagnostic log to every git commit. If the agent ever breaks the build or introduces bloat, you have the exact terminal context of what it was thinking when it made that specific commit.

Here is the complete architectural design and a modular bash script to drive this exact workflow.

The Event-Driven Workflow Architecture

[Agent Working in Tmux]
       │
       ▼ (Modifies roadmap.md)
[Filesystem Watcher (fswatch)] ───► Wakes up Script (Zero Polling)
                                          │
                                          ▼
                         [Settling Gate: Check Bottom 5 Lines]
                         (Loops every 1s until "Working..." clears)
                                          │
                                          ▼
                         [Capture Output -> latest_agent_output.txt]
                         [Git Stage & Commit ("work: milestone")]
                                          │
                                          ▼
                            [Decision Tree Evaluation]
                           Are all '[ ]' boxes checked?
                              /                    \
                         (NO)                        (YES)
                          /                            \
              [Send: "good job, continue"]        [Phase 2 Wrap-Up Sequence]
              [Loop back to Watcher]              1. Clean up loose ends
                                                  2. Project retrospective
                                                  3. Tooling retrospective
                                                  4. Final milestone commit

The Orchestrator Script

This script uses fswatch (a cross-platform file monitor available via Homebrew or apt) to block execution until the roadmap changes, zeroing out CPU usage while waiting.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

TARGET_PANE="my_session:0.0"
ROADMAP_FILE="roadmap.md"
OUTPUT_LOG="latest_agent_output.txt"

# --- HELPER FUNCTIONS ---

# 1. The Settling Gate: Waits until the agent UI clears the "Working..." spinner
wait_for_agent_idle() {
  echo "Roadmap modified. Waiting for terminal output to settle..."
  while true; do
    # Capture the bottom 5 lines of the pane, stripping ANSI colors
    BOTTOM_LINES=$(tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -5)
    
    # Adjust the regex to match your specific agent's active spinner/timer text
    # e.g., matching "Working...", "Esc[...m", or time elapsed like "2m 14s"
    if ! echo "$BOTTOM_LINES" | grep -i -E "(working|esc to cancel|[0-9]+m [0-9]+s)"; then
      # Give it 1 final second to ensure rendering is completely done
      sleep 1
      break
    fi
    sleep 1
  done
  echo "Agent is idle."
}

# 2. State Capture: Grabs scrollback buffer and overwrites the log file
save_agent_output() {
  # Capture the last 500 lines of scrollback (adjust as needed for context depth)
  tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -500 > "$OUTPUT_LOG"
}

# 3. Commit Helper: Stages all changes, the log, and commits
commit_state() {
  local COMMIT_MSG="$1"
  git add .
  git commit -m "$COMMIT_MSG"
}

# 4. Phase 2 Step Executor: Sends prompt, waits for idle, captures, and commits
run_wrapup_step() {
  local PROMPT="$1"
  local COMMIT_MSG="$2"
  
  echo "Executing Wrap-Up Step: $COMMIT_MSG"
  tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" "$PROMPT" C-m
  
  # Brief pause to allow the agent to start "Working..." before we check idle state
  sleep 3 
  
  wait_for_agent_idle
  save_agent_output
  commit_state "$COMMIT_MSG"
}

# --- MAIN DECISION LOOP ---

echo "Starting Agent Orchestrator. Watching $ROADMAP_FILE..."

while true; do
  # Block execution until roadmap.md is modified (-1 means exit after 1 event)
  fswatch -1 "$ROADMAP_FILE" > /dev/null
  
  # Step 1: Wait for terminal text to settle
  wait_for_agent_idle
  
  # Step 2: Save terminal state and make standard work commit
  save_agent_output
  commit_state "work: milestone progression"
  
  # Step 3: Decision Tree - Check if any incomplete milestones '[ ]' remain
  if grep -q "\[ \]" "$ROADMAP_FILE"; then
    echo "Milestones remaining. Sending encouragement..."
    tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" "good job, please continue" C-m
  else
    echo "All milestones complete! Entering Phase 2 Wrap-Up Sequence..."
    
    # Step 4: Phase 2 Sequential Execution
    run_wrapup_step "Please clean up any temporary files, remove debug logs, and finish any loose ends in the codebase." "chore: agent cleanup and loose ends"
    
    run_wrapup_step "Please write a comprehensive project retrospective documenting the architecture and decisions made." "docs: project retrospective"
    
    run_wrapup_step "Please write a tooling-retrospective detailing what prompts, tools, or missing capabilities could have helped you complete this faster." "docs: tooling retrospective"
    
    echo "Project roadmap and wrap-up sequence fully completed!"
    break
  fi
done

Why This Fits Your "Clean Room" Philosophy

Because you prefer starting fresh on new branches to eliminate bloat, this architecture gives you two massive advantages at the end of the run:

  1. The Commit Log is a Timeline: You can git log --stat and see exactly which milestone introduced a specific file change, alongside the latest_agent_output.txt explaining the agent's rationale at that exact moment.
  2. The Tooling Retrospective is Isolated: By making the tooling retrospective the very last commit in Phase 2, you can easily extract that single markdown file to refine your global system prompts for your next clean-room branch without dragging along any codebase bloat.

turns.prompt_text: How can I add error and stall detection to this bash script so it alerts me if the CLI agent gets stuck or outputs an error in the tmux pane?
turns.response_html:
To prevent an unattended agent from burning tokens in an endless error loop or sitting dead for hours, you need to add three guardrails to your script:

  1. A Background Watchdog Timer: Prevents fswatch from blocking indefinitely if the agent stalls out before completing a milestone.
  2. Active Error Pattern Matching: Scrapes the pane while waiting for the roadmap to update, catching API rate limits, syntax crashes, or CLI exceptions immediately.
  3. Multi-Modal Alerting: Triggers an immediate audio beep, dumps an emergency diagnostic log, and fires a native desktop popup notification so you get alerted even if Alacritty is minimized or on another workspace.

Here is the upgraded orchestrator script with integrated stall and error detection:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

TARGET_PANE="my_session:0.0"
ROADMAP_FILE="roadmap.md"
OUTPUT_LOG="latest_agent_output.txt"

# --- TIMEOUT THRESHOLDS (in seconds) ---
WORK_TIMEOUT=1800  # 30 minutes max to complete a single milestone
IDLE_TIMEOUT=300   # 5 minutes max for "Working..." spinner to clear after edit

# --- ALERT & EMERGENCY DUMP ---

trigger_alert() {
  local REASON="$1"
  echo "=================================================="
  echo " [!] ALERT TRIGGERED: $REASON"
  echo "=================================================="
  
  # 1. Capture emergency diagnostic dump of the entire scrollback buffer
  local DUMP_FILE="error_dump_$(date +%s).log"
  tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -1000 > "$DUMP_FILE"
  echo "Emergency state saved to: $DUMP_FILE"
  
  # 2. Terminal audio bell
  printf "\a"
  
  # 3. Native Desktop Notification (macOS / Linux compatible)
  if command -v osascript &> /dev/null; then
    osascript -e "display notification \"$REASON\" with title \"AI Agent Alert\" sound name \"Ping\""
  elif command -v notify-send &> /dev/null; then
    notify-send --urgency=critical "AI Agent Alert" "$REASON"
  fi
}

# --- ERROR PATTERN SCRAPER ---

check_pane_for_errors() {
  # Capture bottom 15 lines where CLI crash logs or API errors appear
  local BUFFER
  BUFFER=$(tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -15)
  
  # Specific CLI/API crash signatures (avoid general words like "error" to prevent false positives during coding)
  if echo "$BUFFER" | grep -i -E "(rate limit exceeded|api_key|traceback \(most recent|syntaxerror:|fatal error:|out of memory|failed to compile|context length exceeded)"; then
    return 0 # Error found
  fi
  return 1 # No error
}

# --- WATCHDOG WAITER FUNCTIONS ---

# 1. Dual-Loop Watchdog: Waits for roadmap edit WHILE checking for errors/stalls
wait_for_roadmap_update() {
  echo "Watching $ROADMAP_FILE (Timeout: ${WORK_TIMEOUT}s)..."
  local ELAPSED=0
  
  # Run fswatch in the background so we aren't blocked forever
  fswatch -1 "$ROADMAP_FILE" > /dev/null 2>&1 &
  local FSWATCH_PID=$!
  
  while kill -0 "$FSWATCH_PID" 2>/dev/null; do
    # Check for CLI crash/error while the agent is working
    if check_pane_for_errors; then
      kill "$FSWATCH_PID" 2>/dev/null
      trigger_alert "Active error or crash pattern detected in tmux pane!"
      return 1
    fi
    
    # Check if the agent has exceeded the maximum milestone duration
    if [ $ELAPSED -ge $WORK_TIMEOUT ]; then
      kill "$FSWATCH_PID" 2>/dev/null
      trigger_alert "Stall Detected: No roadmap update in $WORK_TIMEOUT seconds."
      return 1
    fi
    
    sleep 5
    ((ELAPSED+=5))
  done
  
  return 0 # Roadmap was modified successfully
}

# 2. Settling Gate with Spinner Timeout
wait_for_agent_idle() {
  echo "Roadmap modified. Waiting for terminal output to settle..."
  local ELAPSED=0
  
  while true; do
    if check_pane_for_errors; then
      trigger_alert "Error detected while waiting for agent to settle!"
      return 1
    fi
    
    local BOTTOM_LINES
    BOTTOM_LINES=$(tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -5)
    
    # Check if active spinner/timer has cleared
    if ! echo "$BOTTOM_LINES" | grep -i -E "(working|esc to cancel|[0-9]+m [0-9]+s)"; then
      sleep 1 # Final 1-second render buffer
      break
    fi
    
    if [ $ELAPSED -ge $IDLE_TIMEOUT ]; then
      trigger_alert "Stall Detected: Agent spinner active for over $IDLE_TIMEOUT seconds."
      return 1
    fi
    
    sleep 1
    ((ELAPSED++))
  done
  echo "Agent is idle."
  return 0
}

# --- STATE MANAGEMENT ---

save_agent_output() {
  tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -500 > "$OUTPUT_LOG"
}

commit_state() {
  local COMMIT_MSG="$1"
  git add .
  git commit -m "$COMMIT_MSG"
}

run_wrapup_step() {
  local PROMPT="$1"
  local COMMIT_MSG="$2"
  
  echo "Executing Wrap-Up Step: $COMMIT_MSG"
  tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" "$PROMPT" C-m
  sleep 3 
  
  if wait_for_agent_idle; then
    save_agent_output
    commit_state "$COMMIT_MSG"
  else
    echo "Wrap-up step aborted due to alert!"
    exit 1
  fi
}

# --- MAIN ORCHESTRATOR LOOP ---

echo "Starting Agent Orchestrator with Guardrails..."

while true; do
  # Step 1: Wait for roadmap edit with background watchdog & error scraping
  if ! wait_for_roadmap_update; then
    echo "Orchestrator paused due to stall or error. Fix the pane and restart."
    exit 1
  fi
  
  # Step 2: Wait for terminal text to settle
  if ! wait_for_agent_idle; then
    echo "Orchestrator paused due to UI hang. Fix the pane and restart."
    exit 1
  fi
  
  # Step 3: Save terminal state and make standard work commit
  save_agent_output
  commit_state "work: milestone progression"
  
  # Step 4: Decision Tree - Check remaining milestones
  if grep -q "\[ \]" "$ROADMAP_FILE"; then
    echo "Milestones remaining. Sending encouragement..."
    tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" "good job, please continue" C-m
  else
    echo "All milestones complete! Entering Phase 2 Wrap-Up Sequence..."
    
    run_wrapup_step "Please clean up any temporary files, remove debug logs, and finish any loose ends in the codebase." "chore: agent cleanup and loose ends"
    run_wrapup_step "Please write a comprehensive project retrospective documenting the architecture and decisions made." "docs: project retrospective"
    run_wrapup_step "Please write a tooling-retrospective detailing what prompts, tools, or missing capabilities could have helped you complete this faster." "docs: tooling retrospective"
    
    echo "Project roadmap and wrap-up sequence fully completed!"
    break
  fi
done

Key Architectural Decisions

1. The Non-Blocking Watchdog (kill -0)

Standard fswatch -1 freezes the script until a file change occurs, meaning if the agent crashes hard and stops writing to the disk, your script hangs forever. By spinning fswatch into a background process (&) and checking its PID (kill -0) inside a loop, the script retains control. It can actively poll the pane for errors every 5 seconds while waiting for the filesystem event to trigger.

2. Specific Error Regex vs. General Keywords

If you grep for words like "error" or "failed", the script will false-alarm the moment the agent writes a markdown file about error handling or writes a try/catch block in code. The regex in check_pane_for_errors strictly targets runtime exceptions, API rate limit rejections, and fatal compiler crashes.

3. Emergency State Preservation

When an alert triggers, the script immediately dumps the last 1,000 lines of scrollback to a timestamped file (error_dump_<timestamp>.log) before halting. This ensures that even if you manually interact with the terminal or restart the session to debug, the exact stack trace and agent reasoning at the moment of failure are preserved for your records.

turns.response_html:
This is a brilliant optimization. Treating milestone completion as a statistical probability distribution rather than a flat guessing game allows you to eliminate terminal IPC noise almost entirely during the early stages of a task.

By recording the duration of each milestone to a local project file (e.g., .milestone_telemetry.log), your script can dynamically calculate the expected time to completion ($\mu$) and adapt its polling rate based on where the agent is in the execution curve.

The 3-Tier Adaptive Polling Schedule

Instead of hitting tmux capture-pane every 5 seconds, the watchdog divides the timeline into three distinct operational zones based on the historical average duration (AVG_DUR):

[0% - 50% of Expected Time] ──► GRACE PERIOD: Poll every 15-30s (Only checking for instant crashes)
[50% - 100% of Expected Time] ─► APPROACH WINDOW: Poll every 5s (Standard monitoring)
[> 100% of Expected Time] ────► OVERTIME WINDOW: Poll every 2s (High-frequency stall/finish detection)

If your milestones historically take 10 minutes (600 seconds), the script will only check the pane 4 or 5 times during the first 5 minutes. As it enters the expected completion window, it tightens the loop automatically.

The Upgraded Telemetry & Watchdog Functions

You can drop these upgraded functions directly into your existing orchestrator script. It uses standard awk to calculate averages on the fly without external dependencies.

TELEMETRY_FILE=".milestone_telemetry.log"

# --- TELEMETRY ENGINE ---

# 1. Calculate historical average milestone duration (in seconds)
get_expected_duration() {
  if [ -f "$TELEMETRY_FILE" ] && [ -s "$TELEMETRY_FILE" ]; then
    # Calculate integer mean from historical logs
    awk '{sum+=$1} END {if (NR>0) print int(sum/NR); else print 120}' "$TELEMETRY_FILE"
  else
    echo 120 # Default fallback: 2 minutes if no history exists yet
  fi
}

# 2. Record completed milestone duration to project history
record_telemetry() {
  local DURATION="$1"
  echo "$DURATION" >> "$TELEMETRY_FILE"
  echo "Telemetry updated: Recorded milestone duration of ${DURATION}s."
}

# --- ADAPTIVE WATCHDOG ---

wait_for_roadmap_update() {
  local START_TIME
  START_TIME=$(date +%s)
  
  local AVG_DUR
  AVG_DUR=$(get_expected_duration)
  
  echo "Watching $ROADMAP_FILE (Historical Average: ${AVG_DUR}s | Max Timeout: ${WORK_TIMEOUT}s)..."
  
  # Launch fswatch in the background
  fswatch -1 "$ROADMAP_FILE" > /dev/null 2>&1 &
  local FSWATCH_PID=$!
  
  while kill -0 "$FSWATCH_PID" 2>/dev/null; do
    local NOW
    NOW=$(date +%s)
    local ELAPSED=$((NOW - START_TIME))
    
    # Check for fatal CLI crashes or errors
    if check_pane_for_errors; then
      kill "$FSWATCH_PID" 2>/dev/null
      trigger_alert "Active error or crash pattern detected in tmux pane!"
      return 1
    fi
    
    # Check for hard timeout
    if [ $ELAPSED -ge $WORK_TIMEOUT ]; then
      kill "$FSWATCH_PID" 2>/dev/null
      trigger_alert "Stall Detected: No roadmap update in $WORK_TIMEOUT seconds."
      return 1
    fi
    
    # --- DYNAMIC TACTFUL POLLING CALCULATION ---
    local POLL_INTERVAL
    if [ $ELAPSED -lt $((AVG_DUR * 50 / 100)) ]; then
      # GRACE PERIOD (0% - 50% of average time): Very slow polling
      POLL_INTERVAL=$((AVG_DUR * 15 / 100))
      [ $POLL_INTERVAL -lt 15 ] && POLL_INTERVAL=15 # Floor at 15 seconds
    elif [ $ELAPSED -lt $AVG_DUR ]; then
      # APPROACH WINDOW (50% - 100% of average time): Standard polling
      POLL_INTERVAL=5
    else
      # OVERTIME WINDOW (> 100% of average time): Aggressive polling
      POLL_INTERVAL=2
    fi
    
    # Sleep for the calculated dynamic interval before checking again
    sleep "$POLL_INTERVAL"
  done
  
  # Record the total elapsed time to improve future statistical predictions
  local END_TIME
  END_TIME=$(date +%s)
  record_telemetry $((END_TIME - START_TIME))
  
  return 0
}

Why This Improves the Workflow

  1. Zero Early-Milestone Friction: When an agent begins a complex milestone, it often spends several minutes reading files, running diffs, and synthesizing code. Hitting tmux capture-pane during this phase is wasted compute. The Grace Period lets the system breathe while still maintaining a 15–30 second safety net for immediate syntax or API key crashes.
  2. Self-Calibrating per Project: A simple HTML landing page project will naturally establish a 45-second average duration, tightening the polling loop quickly. A complex C++ refactoring project might establish a 15-minute average, automatically expanding the grace period to 7.5 minutes of complete background silence.
  3. Outlier Detection: By logging the raw seconds to .milestone_telemetry.log, you can later pipe that file into a script or spreadsheet to analyze which milestones caused the agent to struggle and optimize your future roadmap prompting strategies accordingly.

turns.response_html:
The Clean-Room Agent Methodology

This framework treats local CLI agents (like Codex or Antigravity) not as open-ended conversationalists, but as deterministic, time-boxed workers operating within a strictly controlled execution environment.

By binding the agent's workspace to an Alacritty TMUX pane and orchestrating it via an external bash manager, you eliminate the cognitive overload of multi-project terminal tracking and prevent the codebase from accumulating bloat.

Core Philosophical Pillars

1. Clean-Room Execution & Anti-Bloat

AI agents degrade over long conversational horizons. They hallucinate constraints, build convoluted workarounds, and leave behind orphaned code.

  • The Rule: Never continue a project past the initial roadmap. Once a roadmap completes, the branch is evaluated, lessons and modular components are harvested, and the next iteration starts from scratch on a clean git branch.
  • The Benefit: Zero bloat accumulation. Your architecture remains intentional, not reactive.

2. Plaintext State as the Source of Truth

The agent's progress is not stored in an opaque SQLite database or internal agent memory—it lives entirely in the filesystem.

  • The Rule: A plaintext roadmap.md file containing checkable Markdown task lists ([ ] vs [x]) is the single source of truth. When the agent finishes a unit of work, its final action must be checking off that box and saving the file.
  • The Benefit: Filesystem modifications are deterministic and universally observable by basic bash utilities.

3. The Immutable Audit Trail

Code commits without context are difficult to debug when an agent introduces a subtle flaw.

  • The Rule: Every git commit triggered by the orchestrator must bundle the staged code changes with a snapshot of the agent's terminal scrollback (latest_agent_output.txt).
  • The Benefit: If a milestone breaks the build, git log reveals not just the diff, but the exact reasoning, tool outputs, and execution trace of the agent at that exact second.

4. Tactful, Self-Calibrating Automation

Brute-force polling wastes CPU cycles and generates unnecessary terminal noise.

  • The Rule: The manager relies on event-driven filesystem watching (fswatch) as its primary trigger. Terminal buffer scraping is used exclusively as an asynchronous watchdog, utilizing historical project telemetry to dynamically scale its polling rate (Grace Period $\rightarrow$ Approach Window $\rightarrow$ Overtime).

5. The Two-Phase Lifecycle

  • Phase 1: Progression Loop: The manager provides positive reinforcement ("good job, please continue") and commits state after every checked milestone box.
  • Phase 2: Wrap-Up & Meta-Learning: Once all boxes are checked, the manager shifts from coding to cleanup and extraction, forcing the agent to clean loose ends, document architectural decisions, and record a tooling retrospective to improve your global prompts for the next clean-room run.

System Architecture

                 (Agent actively coding & reading files)
                                   │

[fswatch Background Process] ───► Wakes Up Main Orchestrator Loop

      • Sleeps dynamically         ├───► [Settling Gate] (Waits for "Working..." to clear)
      • Checks syntax/crash regex  │

                                   │

                        /                    \

[Send: "good job, please continue"]    [Phase 2 Wrap-Up Sequence]
[Loop back to Watcher]                 1. Send: Cleanup loose ends -> Commit

Complete Reference Implementation

Save this as agent_orchestrator.sh, make it executable (chmod +x agent_orchestrator.sh), and run it from your project root alongside your roadmap.md.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ==============================================================================
# CLEAN-ROOM AGENT ORCHESTRATOR
# Event-driven, self-calibrating TMUX manager for local CLI agents.
# ==============================================================================

# --- CONFIGURATION ---
TARGET_PANE="my_session:0.0"       # Target TMUX session:window.pane
ROADMAP_FILE="roadmap.md"          # Source of truth for task completion
OUTPUT_LOG="latest_agent_output.txt" # Snapshot log attached to every commit
TELEMETRY_FILE=".milestone_telemetry.log" # Historical duration tracking

# --- THRESHOLDS ---
WORK_TIMEOUT=1800                  # Max seconds allowed per milestone (30 min)
IDLE_TIMEOUT=300                   # Max seconds to wait for UI spinner to clear

# ==============================================================================
# UTILITY & ALERTING FUNCTIONS
# ==============================================================================

trigger_alert() {
  local REASON="$1"
  echo "=================================================="
  echo " [!] EMERGENCY ALERT: $REASON"
  echo "=================================================="
  
  # Dump terminal state for debugging before exiting
  local DUMP_FILE="error_dump_$(date +%s).log"
  tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -1000 > "$DUMP_FILE" 2>/dev/null
  echo "Emergency scrollback saved to: $DUMP_FILE"
  
  # Audio bell
  printf "\a"
  
  # Cross-platform desktop notification
  if command -v osascript &> /dev/null; then
    osascript -e "display notification \"$REASON\" with title \"AI Agent Alert\" sound name \"Ping\""
  elif command -v notify-send &> /dev/null; then
    notify-send --urgency=critical "AI Agent Alert" "$REASON"
  fi
}

check_pane_for_errors() {
  # Scrape bottom 15 lines for fatal CLI exceptions or API rejections
  local BUFFER
  BUFFER=$(tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -15 2>/dev/null)
  
  if echo "$BUFFER" | grep -i -E "(rate limit exceeded|api_key|traceback \(most recent|syntaxerror:|fatal error:|out of memory|failed to compile|context length exceeded)"; then
    return 0 # Error found
  fi
  return 1 # No error
}

save_agent_output() {
  tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -500 > "$OUTPUT_LOG" 2>/dev/null
}

commit_state() {
  local COMMIT_MSG="$1"
  git add .
  git commit -m "$COMMIT_MSG"
}

# ==============================================================================
# TELEMETRY ENGINE
# ==============================================================================

get_expected_duration() {
  if [ -f "$TELEMETRY_FILE" ] && [ -s "$TELEMETRY_FILE" ]; then
    awk '{sum+=$1} END {if (NR>0) print int(sum/NR); else print 120}' "$TELEMETRY_FILE"
  else
    echo 120 # Default fallback: 2 minutes
  fi
}

record_telemetry() {
  local DURATION="$1"
  echo "$DURATION" >> "$TELEMETRY_FILE"
  echo "[-] Telemetry recorded: Milestone completed in ${DURATION}s."
}

# ==============================================================================
# ADAPTIVE WATCHDOG & SETTLING GATES
# ==============================================================================

wait_for_roadmap_update() {
  local START_TIME
  START_TIME=$(date +%s)
  
  local AVG_DUR
  AVG_DUR=$(get_expected_duration)
  
  echo "[-] Watching $ROADMAP_FILE (Historical Avg: ${AVG_DUR}s | Max Timeout: ${WORK_TIMEOUT}s)..."
  
  # Launch fswatch asynchronously so the watchdog loop retains control
  fswatch -1 "$ROADMAP_FILE" > /dev/null 2>&1 &
  local FSWATCH_PID=$!
  
  while kill -0 "$FSWATCH_PID" 2>/dev/null; do
    local NOW
    NOW=$(date +%s)
    local ELAPSED=$((NOW - START_TIME))
    
    # Guardrail 1: Active error pattern detection
    if check_pane_for_errors; then
      kill "$FSWATCH_PID" 2>/dev/null
      trigger_alert "Fatal exception or crash detected in TMUX pane!"
      return 1
    fi
    
    # Guardrail 2: Hard stall timeout
    if [ $ELAPSED -ge $WORK_TIMEOUT ]; then
      kill "$FSWATCH_PID" 2>/dev/null
      trigger_alert "Stall detected: No roadmap update in $WORK_TIMEOUT seconds."
      return 1
    fi
    
    # --- Tactful Adaptive Polling Calculation ---
    local POLL_INTERVAL
    if [ $ELAPSED -lt $((AVG_DUR * 50 / 100)) ]; then
      # Grace Period (0-50% of avg): Low-frequency polling
      POLL_INTERVAL=$((AVG_DUR * 15 / 100))
      [ $POLL_INTERVAL -lt 15 ] && POLL_INTERVAL=15
    elif [ $ELAPSED -lt $AVG_DUR ]; then
      # Approach Window (50-100% of avg): Standard polling
      POLL_INTERVAL=5
    else
      # Overtime Window (>100% of avg): High-frequency polling
      POLL_INTERVAL=2
    fi
    
    sleep "$POLL_INTERVAL"
  done
  
  local END_TIME
  END_TIME=$(date +%s)
  record_telemetry $((END_TIME - START_TIME))
  
  return 0
}

wait_for_agent_idle() {
  echo "[-] Roadmap modified. Waiting for terminal rendering to settle..."
  local ELAPSED=0
  
  while true; do
    if check_pane_for_errors; then
      trigger_alert "Error detected while waiting for agent UI to settle!"
      return 1
    fi
    
    local BOTTOM_LINES
    BOTTOM_LINES=$(tmux capture-pane -p -t "$TARGET_PANE" -S -5 2>/dev/null)
    
    # Ensure active spinners, timers, or "Working..." prompts have cleared
    if ! echo "$BOTTOM_LINES" | grep -i -E "(working|esc to cancel|[0-9]+m [0-9]+s)"; then
      sleep 1 # Final 1-second render buffer
      break
    fi
    
    if [ $ELAPSED -ge $IDLE_TIMEOUT ]; then
      trigger_alert "Stall detected: UI spinner active for over $IDLE_TIMEOUT seconds."
      return 1
    fi
    
    sleep 1
    ((ELAPSED++))
  done
  echo "[-] Agent is idle."
  return 0
}

run_wrapup_step() {
  local PROMPT="$1"
  local COMMIT_MSG="$2"
  
  echo "=================================================="
  echo " [Phase 2] Executing: $COMMIT_MSG"
  echo "=================================================="
  
  tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" "$PROMPT" C-m
  sleep 3 # Allow agent process to spin up before checking idle state
  
  if wait_for_agent_idle; then
    save_agent_output
    commit_state "$COMMIT_MSG"
  else
    echo "[!] Wrap-up step aborted due to alert."
    exit 1
  fi
}

# ==============================================================================
# MAIN ORCHESTRATION LOOP
# ==============================================================================

echo "=================================================="
echo " Starting Clean-Room Orchestrator"
echo " Target Pane: $TARGET_PANE | Roadmap: $ROADMAP_FILE"
echo "=================================================="

# Verify initial setup
if [ ! -f "$ROADMAP_FILE" ]; then
  echo "[!] Error: $ROADMAP_FILE not found in current directory."
  exit 1
fi

while true; do
  # --- PHASE 1: EXECUTION & PROGRESSION ---
  if ! wait_for_roadmap_update; then
    echo "[!] Orchestrator halted due to watchdog alert. Resolve pane state and restart."
    exit 1
  fi
  
  if ! wait_for_agent_idle; then
    echo "[!] Orchestrator halted due to UI hang. Resolve pane state and restart."
    exit 1
  fi
  
  save_agent_output
  commit_state "work: milestone progression"
  
  # --- DECISION GATE ---
  if grep -q "\[ \]" "$ROADMAP_FILE"; then
    echo "[-] Uncompleted milestones detected. Sending positive reinforcement..."
    tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" "good job, please continue" C-m
  else
    echo "=================================================="
    echo " [!] All milestones complete! Entering Phase 2..."
    echo "=================================================="
    
    # --- PHASE 2: WRAP-UP & META-LEARNING ---
    run_wrapup_step \
      "Please clean up any temporary files, remove debug logs, and finish any loose ends in the codebase." \
      "chore: agent cleanup and loose ends"
      
    run_wrapup_step \
      "Please write a comprehensive project retrospective documenting the architecture, core logic, and technical decisions made." \
      "docs: project retrospective"
      
    run_wrapup_step \
      "Please write a tooling-retrospective detailing what prompts, CLI commands, or missing capabilities could have helped you complete this faster or cleaner." \
      "docs: tooling retrospective"
      
    echo "=================================================="
    echo " [✔] Clean-Room cycle complete! Standby for review."
    echo "=================================================="
    break
  fi
done

Operational Best Practices

  1. Bootstrap with a Strong Roadmap Template: The entire system relies on the agent reliably marking [ ] to [x]. In your initial system prompt or workspace instructions, explicitly state: "You must only work on one milestone at a time. When finished, you must update roadmap.md to check off the completed item before pausing."
  2. Isolate the Retrospectives: Because the tooling retrospective is executed as the very last git commit (docs: tooling retrospective), you can effortlessly extract that single markdown file to refine your global system prompts or Karabiner/TMUX automation scripts without touching the underlying project code.
  3. Handle Branch Transplanting Cleanly: Once the loop terminates, use the insights from docs: project retrospective to identify the core modular files. Copy those specific files to a temporary directory, check out a clean git branch, transplant the modules back in, and discard the heavy execution history.

When tmux send-keys (our prompt injection mechanism) silently fails or doesn't trigger the AI agent, it almost always comes down to one of three culprits: an incorrect target pane ID, TUI input swallowing (bracketed paste mode), or the submit keystroke getting lost.

Here is how to diagnose and fix the injection issue immediately.

Step 1: Verify the Exact Target Pane ID

Hardcoding my_session:0.0 is prone to breaking if you rename sessions, open new windows, or rearrange panes. If the script sends keys to a non-existent target, tmux will either fail silently or dump text into the wrong terminal.

Open your terminal and list all active panes with their exact IDs and current running commands:

tmux list-panes -a -F "#{session_name}:#{window_index}.#{pane_index} | PID: #{pane_pid} | Cmd: #{pane_current_command}"

Look for the pane running your CLI agent (node, python, codex, antigravity, etc.).

The Better Fix: Instead of hardcoding the string, pass the exact target pane dynamically when you launch the orchestrator, or use tmux's built-in environmental variables if running from an adjacent pane in the same window:

# If the agent is in pane 0 and your manager script is running in pane 1 of the same window:
TARGET_PANE=".0"

Step 2: Use Literal Injection (-l) and Separate the Enter Key

Many modern AI CLI tools and Terminal User Interfaces (TUIs) use Bracketed Paste Mode or complex readline libraries. When you send text and C-m (Carriage Return) in the exact same send-keys command, the TUI often treats the C-m as a newline inside a pasted block of text rather than a submission command.

To fix this, split the injection into three distinct actions:

  1. Send the text using the literal flag (-l) so special characters (quotes, slashes, brackets) aren't misinterpreted by the shell.
  2. Add a tiny fractional sleep to let the TUI input buffer settle.
  3. Send an explicit Enter key (or whatever key combination your agent uses to submit).

Replace your tmux send-keys calls with a dedicated helper function:

inject_prompt() {
  local PROMPT="$1"
  
  # 1. Send text literally without parsing special characters
  tmux send-keys -l -t "$TARGET_PANE" "$PROMPT"
  
  # 2. Brief buffer pause (200 milliseconds)
  sleep 0.2
  
  # 3. Send the explicit Enter key
  tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" Enter
}

Now, instead of calling tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" "good job, please continue" C-m, you simply call:

inject_prompt "good job, please continue"

Step 3: Check for Special "Submit" Keystrokes

Depending on the specific CLI platform you are running (Codex, Antigravity, Aider, etc.), a standard Enter key might just insert a newline if the tool supports multi-line prompting.

Test manually in your terminal to see what actually submits a prompt in your agent's UI, and adjust the end of the inject_prompt function accordingly:

If your CLI tool requires...Use this send-keys syntax
Double Enter (e.g., empty line to submit)tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" Enter sleep 0.1; tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" Enter
Ctrl + D (EOF / Submit)tmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" C-d
Alt + Enter / Meta + Entertmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" M-Enter
Ctrl + Entertmux send-keys -t "$TARGET_PANE" C-Enter

Quick Diagnostic Test

To isolate the problem right now without waiting for a full roadmap cycle, run this one-liner from another terminal pane, replacing .0 with your agent's actual pane ID:

tmux send-keys -l -t ".0" "test injection" && sleep 0.2 && tmux send-keys -t ".0" Enter

If the text appears in the agent's input box but doesn't submit, you are dealing with a Step 3 (special submit key) issue. If nothing appears at all, you are dealing with a Step 1 (wrong target ID) issue.

turns.response_html:
Moving from TUI screen-scraping to codex app-server (or an equivalent headless RPC/API daemon mode) is a massive architectural upgrade.

When you automate a terminal UI via tmux send-keys and capture-pane, you are essentially building a mechanical turk that has to fight through UI rendering layers, ANSI escape sequences, readline buffers, and bracketed paste modes.

Switching to an app-server model elevates your setup from visual terminal scripting to true systems orchestration.

Why App-Server Mode Wins for Background Automation

FeatureTmux TUI AutomationCodex App-Server (RPC / API)
State DetectionFragile regex scraping of scrollback buffers (grep "Working...").Deterministic event streams (e.g., JSON webhooks, SSE, or WebSocket messages emitting status: "idle").
Prompt InjectionSimulated keystrokes subject to input swallowing or lost Enter keys.Structured API requests (e.g., HTTP POST or JSON-RPC payloads). Zero dropped characters.
Output CaptureRequires guessing line counts (-S -500) and stripping color codes.Clean JSON responses containing exact message history, token usage, and tool execution logs.
Resource OverheadHigh rendering overhead; requires an active terminal emulator attached to a session.True headless daemon that can run quietly in the background without allocating a terminal tty.

How the Architecture Evolves

By utilizing an app-server, your core philosophy—the Clean-Room methodology, filesystem-driven roadmaps, and the two-phase lifecycle—remains 100% intact. What changes is the communication layer between your manager script and the agent.

Instead of your bash orchestrator acting like a pair of hands banging on a keyboard, it becomes an API client talking to a local background service.

[Local File System] ◄─── Read/Write Roadmap ───► [Codex App-Server Daemon]
        │                                                ▲
        ▼ (fswatch event)                                │
[Orchestrator Script] ─── JSON-RPC / HTTP POST ──────────┘
        │                 (e.g., {"prompt": "good job"})
        ▼
[Commit Engine] ◄──────── Pulls Clean Logs via API

1. The "Settling Gate" Becomes an Event Listener

Instead of looping every 1 second to grep the bottom 5 lines of a terminal screen, your orchestrator can query the server's endpoint (or listen to a WebSocket event stream) for the agent's current runtime state:

# Example: Polling a local app-server health/status endpoint
wait_for_server_idle() {
  echo "[-] Waiting for Codex app-server to complete turn..."
  while true; do
    # Query the local API for the agent's execution status
    STATUS=$(curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/status | jq -r '.state')
    
    if [[ "$STATUS" == "idle" || "$STATUS" == "waiting_for_input" ]]; do
      break
    fi
    sleep 2
  done
  echo "[-] Agent is idle."
}

2. Prompt Injection Becomes Bulletproof

No more -l literal flags or fractional sleeps to prevent readline collisions. Sending reinforcement or triggering the Phase 2 wrap-up is a standard HTTP or IPC call:

send_prompt() {
  local TEXT="$1"
  curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/prompt \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"message\": \"$TEXT\", \"stream\": false}" > /dev/null
}

3. Clean-Room Logging is Structured

When you stage your git commit after a milestone completes, you don't have to capture a messy scrollback buffer. You can query the API for the exact conversation transcript since the last commit and save it as a cleanly formatted markdown or JSON file:

save_agent_output() {
  # Grab the last turn's structured response and format it cleanly
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/history?limit=1 | jq -r '.turns[0].output' > "$OUTPUT_LOG"
}

You Still Keep Your TMUX Dashboard

Moving the engine to a background app-server doesn't mean you lose your visual control tower. You can still use Alacritty and TMUX exactly as you like, but with a much cleaner separation of concerns:

  • Pane 0 (The Workspace Watcher): Your standard file tree, git status, or live application preview.
  • Pane 1 (The Roadmap Monitor): A live view of your source of truth (watch -n 2 "cat roadmap.md" or a Markdown viewer).
  • Pane 2 (The Server Logs): Instead of an interactive TUI where keystrokes can get swallowed, you simply stream the raw server logs (tail -f .codex_server.log or a dashboard monitoring the API).

By letting codex app-server handle the heavy lifting in the background via structured IPC, you eliminate 100% of the UI friction while keeping your automated branch-reset and milestone-tracking loop completely bulletproof.

Separating the Agent Communication Layer (talking to codex app-server) from the Workspace Layer (reading roadmap.md and executing Git commands) is the exact right instinct. It enforces the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)—the cornerstone of scalable system design architectures like those taught on DesignGurus.io.

When encapsulating an external daemon or API, your choice between a Singleton, Object-Oriented (OOP) patterns, or a Functional approach determines how painfully your library will scale when you eventually want to run multi-agent workflows or swap underlying AI models.

Why You Should Avoid a Bare Singleton

A Singleton feels intuitive because there is only one "app-server" running in your current terminal. However, in system design, Singletons are glorified global variables that introduce rigid state coupling.

If you design the client as a Singleton today, you lock yourself out of running parallel clean-room branches later (e.g., spinning up Pane A on port 8080 for coding and Pane B on port 8081 for automated testing). Instead of a hardcoded Singleton, pass an instance of your client into your higher-level layers via Dependency Injection.

The DesignGurus Blueprint: Architecture & Patterns

To build a robust, modular base layer that higher orchestrator layers can rely on without breaking, combine three classic structural design patterns:

1. The Adapter Pattern (For the Communication Base Layer)

Instead of hardcoding codex JSON-RPC or HTTP calls directly into your business logic, define an abstract interface (e.g., IAgentClient). You then build a specific CodexAppServerAdapter that implements this interface. If you decide to switch to Antigravity, Ollama, or a custom WebSocket server next month, you simply write a new adapter. The higher-level orchestrator never changes.

2. The Repository Pattern (For the Workspace Responsibility)

As you noted, reading/writing to the workspace is a separate concern. Encapsulate all filesystem reads, roadmap.md box-checking, and Git commands inside a WorkspaceRepository. This layer talks to the disk; the Adapter layer talks to the network.

3. Functional Core, Imperative Shell (For the Orchestrator Layer)

While OOP is great for the adapters and repositories, the actual decision loop—evaluating whether milestones are complete and deciding the next prompt—is best implemented using Functional Programming. Pure functions take the current workspace state and return the next instruction without mutating hidden state.

2. Workspace RepoRepository (OOP)Reads/writes local files and manages version control.get_pending_milestones(), mark_complete(id), commit(msg)
3. Decision EnginePure Functions (Functional)Evaluates state and determines the next progression step.evaluate_next_action(roadmap_state, agent_status)

    def __init__(self, root_dir: str = "."):

To scale this system from a single background script into a multi-agent orchestrator—while supporting real-time streaming protocols (WebSockets/stdio) and stateless burst computing (codex exec)—we need to apply two core system design principles: The Strategy Pattern (for Transport) and The Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Bounded Context.

By completely separating Agent I/O (pure communication) from Workspace State (disk and Git), you ensure that an agent can be hot-swapped, upgraded, or restarted without ever corrupting your version control or project tracking.

The Scalable 3-Tier Architecture

To future-proof for specialized roles (Programmer, Tester, Documenter) without building unnecessary complexity today, we structure the library into three isolated layers:

[Layer 1: Workspace & Git Context]  ◄── Holds State (Files, Roadmap, Git Branch)
                 ▲
                 │ (Injected Dependency)
[Layer 2: Pure Agent I/O]           ◄── Encapsulates Role, Skills & Prompting
                 │
                 ▼ (Strategy Pattern)
[Layer 3: Transport Protocol]       ◄── Stdio, WebSockets, HTTP/REST, or Ephemeral Exec

Key Architectural Decisions for Scaling

  • Protocol Agnosticism (The Transport Strategy): The agent logic should not care how bytes travel. Whether codex app-server is listening via a WebSocket (great for real-time token streaming), stdio (zero-latency local IPC), or an ephemeral codex exec process, the underlying transport is abstracted behind a uniform ITransport interface.
  • State vs. Stateless Execution Modes:
    • Session Mode (app-server via WS/stdio): Long-running, stateful. Used for the core progression loop where context window history matters.
    • Burst Mode (codex exec): Ephemeral, stateless. Used for quick computational tasks (e.g., "format this JSON," "write a regex for X," or "lint this file") without polluting the main session's context window.
  • Role Encapsulation (Future-Proofing): We define an AgentRole metadata tag on the agent base class. While we won't build the routing engine yet, tagging an instance as a TESTER or DOCUMENTER allows future orchestrators to spin up three distinct agents in parallel, all reading from the same Workspace but executing different prompts.

from enum import Enum
from typing import Dict, Any, Optional, Generator

# LAYER 3: TRANSPORT STRATEGY (Protocol Abstraction)

class ITransport(ABC):
    """Abstract strategy for communicating with the underlying AI engine."""
    
    @abstractmethod
    def send(self, payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Send a synchronous message and receive a complete response."""
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def stream(self, payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> Generator[str, None, None]:
        """Yield real-time output chunks (crucial for WebSockets/stdio)."""
        pass
        
    @abstractmethod
    def close(self) -> None:
        """Clean up sockets, file descriptors, or child processes."""
        pass


class StdioTransport(ITransport):
    """Communicates with an app-server daemon via stdin/stdout pipes."""
    def __init__(self, command: str = "codex app-server"):
        # Spawns background process and binds pipes
        pass
    
    def send(self, payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        # Write JSON-RPC to stdin, read response from stdout
        return {"status": "success", "output": "..."}
        
    def stream(self, payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> Generator[str, None, None]:
        # Yield lines from stdout as they arrive
        yield "..."
        
    def close(self) -> None:
        # Terminate child process cleanly
        pass


class WebSocketTransport(ITransport):
    """Communicates via WebSockets for bidirectional real-time streaming."""
    def __init__(self, uri: str = "ws://127.0.0.1:8080"):
        self.uri = uri
        # Initialize WebSocket connection
    
    def send(self, payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        return {"status": "success"}
        
    def stream(self, payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> Generator[str, None, None]:
        yield "..."
        
    def close(self) -> None:
        pass

# =====================================================================

class AgentRole(Enum):
    PROGRAMMER = "programmer"
    TESTER = "tester"
    DOCUMENTER = "documenter"
    GENERAL = "general"


class Agent:
    """
    Pure I/O Agent encapsulation. Knows NOTHING about Git or roadmaps.
    Sole responsibility: Manage conversation state, roles, and execution.
    """
    def __init__(self, role: AgentRole = AgentRole.GENERAL, transport: Optional[ITransport] = None):
        self.role = role
        self.transport = transport
        self.session_id: Optional[str] = None
        
    def prompt(self, message: str, stream: bool = False) -> Any:
        """Stateful turn inside an active app-server session."""
        if not self.transport:
            raise RuntimeError("Session prompting requires an active ITransport.")
            
        payload = {"role": self.role.value, "message": message, "session_id": self.session_id}
        
        if stream:
            return self.transport.stream(payload)
        return self.transport.send(payload)

    @staticmethod
    def exec_once(command: str, prompt: str) -> str:
        """
        STATELESS BURST COMPUTING: Executes a one-off `codex exec` CLI command.
        Spawns a temporary process, gets the result, and terminates immediately.
        Does not use the session transport or pollute the agent's memory.
        """
        full_cmd = [command, "exec", prompt]
        result = subprocess.run(full_cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        return result.stdout.strip()

        self.roadmap_path = f"{root_dir}/roadmap.md"

    async fn stream(&self, payload: Value) -> anyhow::Result<mpsc::Receiver<String>>;
    
    /// Cleanly terminate sockets or child processes.

    transport: Option<Box<dyn Transport>>,
    session_id: Option<String>,

        Self {
            role,
            transport,
            session_id: None,
        }
    }

    /// Execute a stateful turn inside the ongoing app-server session.
    pub async fn prompt(&self, message: &str) -> anyhow::Result<serde_json::Value> {
        let transport = self.transport.as_ref()
            .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("Session prompting requires an active Transport."))?;

        let payload = json!({
            "role": self.role.as_str(),
            "message": message,
            "session_id": self.session_id,
        });

        transport.send(payload).await
    }

    /// STATELESS BURST COMPUTING: Executes a one-off `codex exec` CLI command.
    /// Spawns a temporary OS process, captures stdout, and terminates immediately.
    /// Does not pollute the agent's session memory.
    pub async fn exec_once(cli_bin: &str, prompt: &str) -> anyhow::Result<String> {
        let output = Command::new(cli_bin)
            .arg("exec")
            .arg(prompt)
            .output()
            .await?;

        if !output.status.success() {
            let err_msg = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr);
            anyhow::bail!("Stateless exec failed: {}", err_msg);
        }

        Ok(String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout).trim().to_string())
    }
}

            roadmap_path: root.join("roadmap.md"),
            audit_log_path: root.join("latest_agent_output.txt"),

        let content = fs::read_to_string(&self.roadmap_path).await?;
        Ok(content.matches("[ ]").count())
    }

    /// Stage all files, write the audit log, and commit the milestone.
    pub async fn stage_and_commit(&self, commit_message: &str, audit_log: &str) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        // 1. Write the latest terminal/agent output snapshot
        fs::write(&self.audit_log_path, audit_log).await?;

        // 2. git add .
        let add_status = Command::new("git")
            .arg("add")
            .arg(".")
            .current_dir(&self.root_dir)
            .status()
            .await?;
            
        if !add_status.success() {
            anyhow::bail!("Failed to stage files with git add.");
        }

        // 3. git commit -m "..."
        let commit_status = Command::new("git")
            .args(&["commit", "-m", commit_message])
            .current_dir(&self.root_dir)
            .status()
            .await?;

        if !commit_status.success() {
            anyhow::bail!("Git commit failed.");
        }

        Ok(())
    }

        let status = Command::new("git")
            .args(&["checkout", "-b", branch_name])
            .current_dir(&self.root_dir)
            .status()
            .await?;

        if !status.success() {
            anyhow::bail!("Failed to create clean branch: {}", branch_name);
        }
        Ok(())
    }

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MilestoneStatus {
    Pending,
    InProgress,
    Completed,
    Blocked(String),
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Milestone {
    pub id: String,          // e.g., "M1"
    pub title: String,       // e.g., "Implement JSON-RPC Stdio Transport"
    pub status: MilestoneStatus,
    pub description: Option<String>,
    pub dependencies: Vec<String>, // IDs of prerequisite milestones
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Roadmap {
    pub title: String,
    pub target_branch: String,
    pub milestones: Vec<Milestone>,
}

impl Roadmap {
    /// Deeply grasp progress: Returns true only if all milestones are Completed.
    pub fn is_complete(&self) -> bool {
        !self.milestones.is_empty() && 
        self.milestones.iter().all(|m| m.status == MilestoneStatus::Completed)
    }

    /// Finds the exact next actionable milestone that isn't blocked by dependencies.
    pub fn next_actionable(&self) -> Option<&Milestone> {
        self.milestones.iter().find(|m| {
            m.status == MilestoneStatus::Pending && 
            m.dependencies.iter().all(|dep_id| self.is_dependency_met(dep_id))
        })
    }

    fn is_dependency_met(&self, dep_id: &str) -> bool {
        self.milestones.iter().any(|m| m.id == dep_id && m.status == MilestoneStatus::Completed)
    }
}

2. The Rust Interaction Layer (RoadmapController)

This controller acts as the gatekeeper. It holds the Roadmap object representation in memory, handles automatic YAML persistence to a hidden or out-of-band directory, and exposes strict mutation methods that validate business rules before altering state.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
use tokio::fs;
use chrono::Utc;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MilestoneStatus {
    Pending,
    InProgress,
    Completed,
    Blocked(String),
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Milestone {
    pub id: String,
    pub title: String,
    pub status: MilestoneStatus,
    pub dependencies: Vec<String>,
    pub completed_at: Option<String>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Roadmap {
    pub title: String,
    pub target_branch: String,
    pub active_milestone: Option<String>,
    pub milestones: Vec<Milestone>,
}

/// The Gatekeeper: Encapsulates state and prevents illegal agent mutations.
pub struct RoadmapController {
    storage_path: PathBuf,
    state: Roadmap,
}

impl RoadmapController {
    /// Loads the YAML from an out-of-band directory (e.g., ~/.codex_projects/state.yaml)
    pub async fn load<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> anyhow::Result<Self> {
        let content = fs::read_to_string(&path).await?;
        let state: Roadmap = serde_yaml::from_str(&content)?;
        Ok(Self {
            storage_path: path.as_ref().to_path_buf(),
            state,
        })
    }

    /// READ-ONLY ACCESS: Returns a sanitized, read-only view for prompt injection
    pub fn get_active_context_view(&self) -> String {
        let mut view = format!("# Project Roadmap: {}\n\n", self.state.title);
        for m in &self.state.milestones {
            let marker = match m.status {
                MilestoneStatus::Completed => "[✔]",
                MilestoneStatus::InProgress => "[►]",
                MilestoneStatus::Pending => "[ ]",
                MilestoneStatus::Blocked(_) => "[!]",
            };
            view.push_str(&format!("{} {} - {}\n", marker, m.id, m.title));
        }
        view
    }

    /// MUTATION METHOD: Strictly validates transitions before applying changes
    pub async fn complete_milestone(&mut self, target_id: &str) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        // 1. Verify all dependencies are completed
        let target = self.state.milestones.iter()
            .find(|m| m.id == target_id)
            .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("Milestone ID '{}' not found.", target_id))?;

        for dep_id in &target.dependencies {
            let dep_met = self.state.milestones.iter()
                .any(|m| m.id == *dep_id && m.status == MilestoneStatus::Completed);
            if !dep_met {
                anyhow::bail!("Illegal Mutation: Cannot complete '{}' because dependency '{}' is not met.", target_id, dep_id);
            }
        }

        // 2. Apply mutation
        if let Some(m) = self.state.milestones.iter_mut().find(|m| m.id == target_id) {
            m.status = MilestoneStatus::Completed;
            m.completed_at = Some(Utc::now().to_rfc3339());
        }

        // 3. Auto-advance active milestone pointer
        self.advance_active_milestone();

        // 4. Persist immediately to disk
        self.persist().await?;
        Ok(())
    }

    fn advance_active_milestone(&mut self) {
        self.state.active_milestone = self.state.milestones.iter()
            .find(|m| {
                m.status == MilestoneStatus::Pending && 
                m.dependencies.iter().all(|dep| self.is_completed(dep))
            })
            .map(|m| m.id.clone());
    }

    fn is_completed(&self, id: &str) -> bool {
        self.state.milestones.iter()
            .any(|m| m.id == id && m.status == MilestoneStatus::Completed)
    }

    async fn persist(&self) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let yaml_str = serde_yaml::to_string(&self.state)?;
        fs::write(&self.storage_path, yaml_str).await?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

3. Why This Transcends the Old File-Watcher Loop

By shifting from fswatch on a workspace file to an encapsulated Rust controller, your orchestrator loop becomes purely programmatic and event-driven:

  1. Clean-Room Immunity: When your orchestrator wipes the git branch to start Phase 2 (or a new sprint), the YAML state remains untouched in memory or in your out-of-band .project_state/ directory. You never have to manually stash or transplant the roadmap file again.
  2. Deterministic Prompt Injections: At the beginning of each turn, your Rust loop calls controller.get_active_context_view() and prepends it to the agent's prompt. The agent always sees the exact, uncorrupted state of the project without ever needing to read a file from disk.
  3. Architectural Guardrails: If an agent hallucinates that it finished the entire project and tries to call complete_milestone("M3") while M2 is incomplete, the Rust controller throws an error, aborts the state change, and can immediately feed an automated corrective prompt back into the TMUX pane: "Error: Cannot complete M3 until dependency M2 is verified."

1. The 3-Tier Shallow Hierarchy

To enforce "shallowness" and prevent agents from creating infinitely nested sub-tasks, we design the Rust type system so that recursion is structurally impossible. A Milestone contains Tasks, a Task contains SubTasks, and a SubTask is a leaf node.

use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};

2. The Versioning Solution: Event-Sourced Mutation Logs

Why does it feel like you need a "separate Git repository"? Because you need temporal replayability. If Milestone 1 burns through its resource budget ($R_{spent} > R_{budget}$), you want to look back and see: "Ah, the Tester agent injected 14 new sub-tasks at 10:14 AM because it found a regression."

We can achieve 100% Git-like versioning without Git by using an Append-Only Event Journal. Every time an agent amends a task, the Rust controller records an immutable event before updating the snapshot.

[.project_state/]
  ├── roadmap.yaml          ◄── Current materialized snapshot (Fast to read)
  └── roadmap_events.log    ◄── Append-only ledger of every mutation (Our "Shadow Git")

The Rust Mutation Ledger

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum RoadmapMutation {
    TaskAdded {
        milestone_id: String,
        task: Task,
        agent_role: String,
        reason: String,
        timestamp: DateTime<Utc>,
    },
    SubTaskAdded {
        task_id: String,
        subtask: SubTask,
        agent_role: String,
        reason: String,
        timestamp: DateTime<Utc>,
    },
    StatusChanged {
        node_id: String,
        old_status: Status,
        new_status: Status,
        agent_role: String,
        timestamp: DateTime<Utc>,
    },
}

pub struct RoadmapController {
    state: Roadmap,
    journal_path: std::path::PathBuf,
}

impl RoadmapController {
    /// AGENT MUTATION GATEWAY: Enforces strategic immutability while allowing tactical fluidity.
    pub async fn apply_agent_mutation(&mut self, mutation: RoadmapMutation) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        match &mutation {
            RoadmapMutation::TaskAdded { milestone_id, task, .. } => {
                let milestone = self.state.milestones.iter_mut()
                    .find(|m| &m.id == milestone_id)
                    .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("Milestone not found"))?;
                
                // We permit adding tasks, but never altering the milestone itself
                milestone.tasks.push(task.clone());
            },
            RoadmapMutation::SubTaskAdded { task_id, subtask, .. } => {
                // Find task across all milestones and push subtask
                let mut found = false;
                for m in &mut self.state.milestones {
                    if let Some(t) = m.tasks.iter_mut().find(|t| &t.id == task_id) {
                        t.subtasks.push(subtask.clone());
                        found = true;
                        break;
                    }
                }
                if !found { anyhow::bail!("Task ID not found"); }
            },
            // Notice: There are explicitly NO match arms for modifying Milestone titles, 
            // resource boundaries, or deleting strategic goals!
            _ => { /* Handle status updates... */ }
        }

        // 1. Append to the immutable ledger (Our "Shadow Git Commit")
        self.append_to_journal(&mutation).await?;

        // 2. Overwrite the materialized YAML snapshot
        self.persist_snapshot().await?;
        
        Ok(())
    }

    async fn append_to_journal(&self, mutation: &RoadmapMutation) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        use tokio::io::AsyncWriteExt;
        let mut file = tokio::fs::OpenOptions::new()
            .create(true)
            .append(true)
            .open(&self.journal_path)
            .await?;
            
        let json_line = serde_json::to_string(mutation)?;
        file.write_all(format!("{}\n", json_line).as_bytes()).await?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

3. How This Protects Against Scope Creep

By allowing task amendments, you inevitably invite scope creep. However, because you are using Resource Control per Milestone (e.g., token usage, cost, or execution time boundaries) rather than task counts, this hierarchical architecture gives you an automatic circuit breaker:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{Cost}(T_i) \le \text{Budget}_{milestone}$$

  1. The Fluid Phase: The Programmer begins Milestone 1. The Tester agent discovers an edge case and calls rpc:add_subtask, appending a test requirement. The controller allows this, writes to roadmap_events.log, and updates roadmap.yaml.
  2. The Budget Boundary: As the agents work through the amended tasks, the orchestrator monitors total compute expended against milestone.resource_limit_usd.
  3. The Circuit Breaker: If the agents amend too many tasks and hit the resource ceiling, the Rust orchestrator freezes execution immediately—even if tasks are left pending.
  4. The Audit: You don't have to guess why the budget blew up. You can inspect roadmap_events.log to see exactly which agent injected the extra scope and decide whether to increase the budget or reset the branch.

1. Supporting Add, Modify, and Remove Mutations

When you allow agents to remove or modify tasks, you introduce a risk: an agent might delete a failing task just to make the build pass.

To prevent this, our Rust schema mandates that removals and modifications require an explicit justification (reason) and are permanently recorded in the event ledger. An agent can delete a task from the materialized YAML, but it can never delete the record of having deleted it.

2. The Rust Commit-Time Injector

Here is how the WorkspaceContext is upgraded to handle the injection. Right before staging, it dumps the authoritative YAML and append-only event log directly into a .meta/ or root directory inside the Git working tree.

use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
use tokio::fs;
use tokio::process::Command;

pub struct WorkspaceContext {
    root_dir: PathBuf,
    roadmap_path: PathBuf,
    events_log_path: PathBuf,
    terminal_audit_path: PathBuf,
}

impl WorkspaceContext {
    pub fn new<P: AsRef<Path>>(root_dir: P) -> Self {
        let root = root_dir.as_ref().to_path_buf();
        Self {
            roadmap_path: root.join("roadmap.yaml"),
            events_log_path: root.join("roadmap_events.log"),
            terminal_audit_path: root.join("latest_agent_output.txt"),
            root_dir: root,
        }
    }

    /// COMMIT-TIME INJECTION: Overwrites workspace state with authoritative internal memory
    /// before staging and committing to Git.
    pub async fn inject_and_commit(
        &self,
        commit_message: &str,
        authoritative_yaml: &str,
        event_ledger_raw: &str,
        terminal_output: &str,
    ) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        
        // 1. Forcibly inject authoritative out-of-band state into the working directory
        fs::write(&self.roadmap_path, authoritative_yaml).await?;
        fs::write(&self.events_log_path, event_ledger_raw).await?;
        fs::write(&self.terminal_audit_path, terminal_output).await?;

        // 2. Stage all changes (Code diffs + Injected State)
        let add_status = Command::new("git")
            .arg("add")
            .arg(".")
            .current_dir(&self.root_dir)
            .status()
            .await?;

        if !add_status.success() {
            anyhow::bail!("Git add failed during state injection.");
        }

        // 3. Commit with semantic message
        let commit_status = Command::new("git")
            .args(&["commit", "-m", commit_message])
            .current_dir(&self.root_dir)
            .status()
            .await?;

        if !commit_status.success() {
            anyhow::bail!("Git commit failed during state injection.");
        }

        Ok(())
    }
}

Why This Perfects the Clean-Room Loop

  1. Zero State Pollution During Dev: When your Programmer agent is listing directory contents or running pattern searches, it doesn't get confused by sprawling mutation logs or YAML metadata. The workspace contains purely code until the exact second the commit occurs.
  2. Post-Mortem Debugging: If an agent deletes a task (TaskRemoved) and the build suddenly fails two milestones later, you can run a simple git diff or grep on roadmap_events.log in that specific commit: 
    grep "TaskRemoved" roadmap_events.log
# Output: {"TaskRemoved": {"task_id": "M1-T3", "agent_role": "tester", "reason": "Decided unit tests were redundant for abstract trait", "timestamp": "..."}}
    You immediately know which role made the bad call and why, allowing you to tweak your Tester system prompt before spinning up your next clean-room branch.

To make these tools reliable for LLMs (like those powering Codex or Antigravity), your JSON-RPC tool schemas must adhere to three strict API design rules:

  1. Server-Side ID Generation: Never trust an agent to generate its own sequence IDs (e.g., guessing "M1-T4"). If two agents propose the same ID simultaneously, your state corrupts. The agent passes the parent ID ("M1"), and the Rust server auto-generates, attaches, and returns the new deterministic ID in the RPC response.
  2. Server-Injected Authentication: Do not include agent_role in the JSON tool schema. If you ask an LLM to identify its role, a Programmer agent can hallucinate "agent_role": "admin" to bypass guardrails. The Rust transport layer already knows which session belongs to the Programmer, Tester, or Documenter; the server injects the authenticated role into the event ledger automatically.
  3. Mandatory Audit Justifications: Every single mutation schema must require a non-empty reason string. If an agent wants to expand scope or delete a failing test, it must justify why to the event journal.

3. The Rust JSON-RPC Dispatcher & Gatekeeper

When an agent invokes a tool, the JSON-RPC payload hits your Rust transport layer. This dispatcher intercepts the call, extracts the authenticated session role, enforces Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), and generates deterministic sequence IDs before mutating state.

use serde_json::{json, Value};
use crate::agent::AgentRole;
use crate::domain::{RoadmapController, RoadmapMutation, Task, SubTask, Status};
use chrono::Utc;

pub struct RpcDispatcher {
    controller: tokio::sync::Mutex<RoadmapController>,
}

impl RpcDispatcher {
    /// Intercepts tool calls from the TMUX transport pipe, applying RBAC and ID auto-generation.
    pub async fn handle_tool_call(
        &self,
        authenticated_role: AgentRole,
        tool_name: &str,
        params: Value,
    ) -> anyhow::Result<Value> {
        
        let mut controller = self.controller.lock().await;

        match tool_name {
            "roadmap_add_task" => {
                let milestone_id = params["milestone_id"].as_str()
                    .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("Missing milestone_id"))?;
                let title = params["title"].as_str()
                    .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("Missing title"))?;
                let reason = params["reason"].as_str()
                    .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("Missing reason"))?;
                
                let deps = params["dependencies"].as_array()
                    .map(|arr| arr.iter().filter_map(|v| v.as_str().map(|s| s.to_string())).collect())
                    .unwrap_or_default();

                // 1. SERVER-SIDE ID GENERATION: Auto-calculate next sequence (e.g., "M1-T4")
                let new_id = controller.generate_next_task_id(milestone_id)?;

                let new_task = Task {
                    id: new_id.clone(),
                    title: title.to_string(),
                    status: Status::Pending,
                    dependencies: deps,
                    subtasks: vec![],
                    added_by_agent: Some(authenticated_role.as_str().to_string()),
                };

                // 2. CONSTRUCT EVENT LEDGER MUTATION
                let mutation = RoadmapMutation::TaskAdded {
                    milestone_id: milestone_id.to_string(),
                    task: new_task,
                    agent_role: authenticated_role.as_str().to_string(),
                    reason: reason.to_string(),
                    timestamp: Utc::now(),
                };

                // 3. APPLY AND PERSIST
                controller.apply_agent_mutation(mutation).await?;

                // Return the generated ID back to the LLM so it knows what it just created
                Ok(json!({
                    "status": "success",
                    "generated_id": new_id,
                    "message": format!("Task '{}' successfully attached to {}", new_id, milestone_id)
                }))
            },

            "roadmap_set_status" => {
                let node_id = params["node_id"].as_str()
                    .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("Missing node_id"))?;
                let status_str = params["status"].as_str()
                    .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("Missing status"))?;
                let reason = params["reason"].as_str()
                    .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("Missing reason"))?;

                // --- ROLE-BASED ACCESS CONTROL (RBAC) GUARDRAIL ---
                if status_str == "Completed" && authenticated_role == AgentRole::Tester {
                    anyhow::bail!("RBAC Violation: Tester agents are not permitted to mark engineering nodes as Completed.");
                }

                let new_status = match status_str {
                    "Pending" => Status::Pending,
                    "InProgress" => Status::InProgress,
                    "Completed" => Status::Completed,
                    "Blocked" => {
                        let block_reason = params["block_reason"].as_str()
                            .unwrap_or("No block reason provided");
                        Status::Blocked(block_reason.to_string())
                    },
                    _ => anyhow::bail!("Invalid status enum string"),
                };

                let mutation = RoadmapMutation::StatusChanged {
                    node_id: node_id.to_string(),
                    old_status: controller.get_node_status(node_id)?,
                    new_status,
                    agent_role: authenticated_role.as_str().to_string(),
                    timestamp: Utc::now(),
                };

                controller.apply_agent_mutation(mutation).await?;

                Ok(json!({
                    "status": "success",
                    "message": format!("Node '{}' transitioned to {}", node_id, status_str)
                }))
            },

            // Handle roadmap_add_subtask, roadmap_modify_node, and roadmap_remove_node...
            _ => anyhow::bail!("Unknown RPC tool: {}", tool_name),
        }
    }
}

How This Eliminates Scope Creep & Drift

When your Programmer agent is actively working in TMUX and decides it needs to write an extra utility script, it cannot just silently create a file and move on. To track its work in the UI, it must invoke roadmap_add_subtask.

When it calls that tool, it is forced to supply a reason. Your Rust controller logs: [2026-07-28 09:30:12 UTC] [Programmer] Added SubTask M1-T2-S4: "Write JSON schema validator utility" | Reason: "Realized raw string parsing was throwing panic on null bytes."

When your milestone commit occurs, that exact rationale is permanently injected into your Git history via roadmap_events.log. You get complete tactical malleability for your autonomous agents, governed by rigid, programmatic engineering standards.
