Tracking raw cost in dollars is often too abstract for local CLI agents; tracking rolling rate-limit windows (like 5-hour resets and weekly caps) and active wall-clock time is operational survival.

If an autonomous Programmer agent gets stuck in a recursive error-fixing loop, it won't just waste a few cents—it will trigger your 5-hour rate limit or exhaust your weekly quota, locking out your entire workflow and halting your Tester and Documenter agents as well.

To solve this, we introduce the ResourceGovernor into our Rust orchestrator. It acts as a financial and operational circuit breaker that sits between the RpcDispatcher, the Transport layer, and our out-of-band state.

1. The Resource & Quota Domain Model

We must separate Task Consumption (what a specific unit of work burned) from Global Quota State (where your underlying Codex/LLM account currently sits within its rolling windows).

use chrono::{DateTime, Duration, Utc};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

/// Tracks what a specific Task or Milestone has consumed over its lifetime.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct ResourceConsumption {
    pub active_wall_time_seconds: u64,
    pub total_input_tokens: u64,
    pub total_output_tokens: u64,
    pub estimated_cost_usd: f64,
    pub rpc_turn_count: u32,
}

/// Models the underlying AI provider's rate-limiting and quota state.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct QuotaState {
    pub five_hour_window_resets_at: DateTime<Utc>,
    pub five_hour_utilization_percent: f64,
    pub weekly_tokens_remaining: u64,
    pub weekly_resets_available: u8, // Free resets your tier allows
    pub is_currently_throttled: bool,
}

impl QuotaState {
    /// Determines if we are approaching a dangerous threshold where execution should halt.
    pub fn is_in_danger_zone(&self) -> bool {
        self.five_hour_utilization_percent >= 85.0 || self.weekly_tokens_remaining < 50_000
    }
}

2. Intercepting Telemetry at the Transport Layer

When codex app-server executes a turn, its JSON-RPC response payload almost always includes a metadata or usage block, alongside HTTP rate-limit headers (if using HTTP/WebSockets) or system event emissions (if using stdio).

We upgrade our Transport wrapper to strip this telemetry out of every raw response and feed it into our event ledger before returning the output text to the agent.

use serde_json::Value;
use crate::domain::ResourceConsumption;

pub struct TelemetryHarvest {
    pub clean_output: Value,
    pub turn_consumption: ResourceConsumption,
    pub updated_quota: Option<QuotaState>,
}

impl TelemetryHarvest {
    /// Extracts usage metrics from a raw JSON-RPC response payload.
    pub fn from_rpc_response(raw_response: Value, elapsed_time_sec: u64) -> anyhow::Result<Self> {
        let usage = &raw_response["meta"]["usage"];
        
        let turn_consumption = ResourceConsumption {
            active_wall_time_seconds: elapsed_time_sec,
            total_input_tokens: usage["prompt_tokens"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0),
            total_output_tokens: usage["completion_tokens"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0),
            estimated_cost_usd: usage["estimated_cost"].as_f64().unwrap_or(0.0),
            rpc_turn_count: 1,
        };

        // Extract rate limit window data if the server broadcasted it
        let updated_quota = if let Some(quota_val) = raw_response["meta"]["quota_state"].as_object() {
            serde_json::from_value(Value::Object(quota_val.clone())).ok()
        } else {
            None
        };

        Ok(Self {
            clean_output: raw_response["result"].clone(),
            turn_consumption,
            updated_quota,
        })
    }
}

3. The ResourceGovernor & Circuit Breaker

The ResourceGovernor is injected into the orchestrator loop. Before any agent is allowed to execute a prompt or mutate a task, the governor evaluates the remaining budget and quota health. It operates on a 3-Tier Throttle Strategy:

[0% - 75% 5-Hour Utilization]  ──► NORMAL MODE: Full multi-agent execution speed.
[75% - 90% 5-Hour Utilization] ──► CONSERVATION MODE: Suspend Tester/Documenter. Programmer only.
[> 90% 5-Hour Utilization]     ──► CIRCUIT BREAKER TRIPPED: Freeze TMUX panes. Auto-save clean state.

The Rust Governor Implementation

use crate::domain::{QuotaState, ResourceConsumption, RoadmapController};
use chrono::Utc;

pub struct ResourceGovernor {
    quota: QuotaState,
    milestone_budget_usd: f64,
    current_milestone_burn: ResourceConsumption,
}

impl ResourceGovernor {
    pub fn new(initial_quota: QuotaState, milestone_budget_usd: f64) -> Self {
        Self {
            quota: initial_quota,
            milestone_budget_usd,
            current_milestone_burn: ResourceConsumption::default(),
        }
    }

    /// PRE-EXECUTION GATE: Checks if we are allowed to run another prompt turn.
    pub fn authorize_execution(&self) -> anyhow::Result<ExecutionMode> {
        if self.quota.is_currently_throttled {
            anyhow::bail!("Execution halted: Account is currently hard-throttled by provider until {}", 
                self.quota.five_hour_window_resets_at);
        }

        if self.current_milestone_burn.estimated_cost_usd >= self.milestone_budget_usd {
            anyhow::bail!("Circuit Breaker Tripped: Milestone budget of ${:.2} exceeded (Burned: ${:.2}). Scope creep detected!", 
                self.milestone_budget_usd, self.current_milestone_burn.estimated_cost_usd);
        }

        if self.quota.five_hour_utilization_percent >= 90.0 {
            // Check if we have a free reset available before panicking!
            if self.quota.weekly_resets_available > 0 {
                return Ok(ExecutionMode::TriggerFreeReset);
            }
            anyhow::bail!("5-Hour Rolling Limit Critical ({:.1}%). Halting to prevent lockout.", 
                self.quota.five_hour_utilization_percent);
        } else if self.quota.five_hour_utilization_percent >= 75.0 {
            return Ok(ExecutionMode::ConservationMode);
        }

        Ok(ExecutionMode::Normal)
    }

    /// POST-EXECUTION HOOK: Accumulates burn and updates the quota state.
    pub async fn record_burn(
        &mut self, 
        turn_burn: ResourceConsumption, 
        new_quota: Option<QuotaState>,
        controller: &mut RoadmapController,
        active_task_id: &str,
    ) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        
        // 1. Update internal quota state
        if let Some(q) = new_quota {
            self.quota = q;
        }

        // 2. Accumulate milestone burn
        self.current_milestone_burn.active_wall_time_seconds += turn_burn.active_wall_time_seconds;
        self.current_milestone_burn.total_input_tokens += turn_burn.total_input_tokens;
        self.current_milestone_burn.total_output_tokens += turn_burn.total_output_tokens;
        self.current_milestone_burn.estimated_cost_usd += turn_burn.estimated_cost_usd;
        self.current_milestone_burn.rpc_turn_count += 1;

        // 3. Write burn directly to the active Task in the YAML representation
        controller.add_task_telemetry(active_task_id, &turn_burn).await?;

        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum ExecutionMode {
    Normal,
    ConservationMode, // Suspend non-essential agents
    TriggerFreeReset, // Invoke API to claim a free 5-hour window reset
}

Why This Complete Architecture is Bulletproof

You now have a fully realized, production-grade system design that bridges the gap between raw LLM behavior and strict systems engineering:

  1. Clean-Room Immunity: By starting fresh on new branches and wiping the working tree at the end of each roadmap, your codebase never accumulates orphaned bloat.
  2. Out-of-Band State Security: By storing roadmap.yaml, roadmap_events.log, and quota states in memory and injecting them only at commit-time, agents can never alter their own strategic directives or forge completion records.
  3. Malleable Tactical Execution: By utilizing JSON-RPC tool boundaries (add_task, add_subtask, remove_node), Programmer, Tester, and Documenter agents can adapt to real-world coding friction dynamically, with every single pivot permanently justified in the audit trail.

This is the ultimate payoff of using the Strategy Pattern in our Rust transport layer and keeping state out-of-band. Because our RoadmapController, ResourceGovernor, and WorkspaceContext never interact directly with an LLM's raw API—only through our abstract traits—adding Anthropic's Claude, xAI's Grok, or GitHub Copilot CLI is completely frictionless.

To make the architecture genuinely provider-agnostic without bloating the core logic, we need to generalize two specific boundaries: Tool Schema Translation and Polymorphic Quota Accounting.

1. The Provider-Agnostic Transport & Tool Mapper

Different AI CLI tools and APIs consume function calls differently. While Codex and Antigravity (agy) natively speak JSON-RPC or OpenAI-style function schemas, Claude relies on Anthropic's distinct Tool Use structure (or XML tags in older CLI wrappers), and GitHub Copilot CLI often relies on shell-level flag injections or interactive terminal prompts.

Instead of rewriting our RPC tools for every provider, we implement a ToolSchemaMapper inside the Transport implementation. The core Rust engine only ever knows our standardized JSON schema; the provider adapter translates it on the wire.

use serde_json::Value;
use async_trait::async_trait;
use crate::transport::Transport;
use tokio::sync::mpsc;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum ProviderKind {
    Codex,
    Antigravity,
    Claude,
    Grok,
    Copilot,
}

/// Transforms our internal JSON-RPC schemas into whatever wire format the provider demands.
pub struct ProviderAdapter {
    pub kind: ProviderKind,
    pub binary_path: String,
}

impl ProviderAdapter {
    pub fn format_tools_payload(&self, internal_tools: &[Value]) -> Value {
        match self.kind {
            ProviderKind::Codex | ProviderKind::Antigravity | ProviderKind::Grok => {
                // OpenAI/MCP standard format
                serde_json::json!({ "tools": internal_tools })
            },
            ProviderKind::Claude => {
                // Translate JSON Schema properties to Anthropic Tool Use format
                let claude_tools: Vec<Value> = internal_tools.iter().map(|t| {
                    serde_json::json!({
                        "name": t["function"]["name"],
                        "description": t["function"]["description"],
                        "input_schema": t["function"]["parameters"]
                    })
                }).collect();
                serde_json::json!({ "tools": claude_tools })
            },
            ProviderKind::Copilot => {
                // Copilot CLI might require flat prompt instruction injection if tools aren't natively supported
                serde_json::json!({ "system_override": "Use these explicit markdown commands..." })
            }
        }
    }
}

2. Polymorphic Quota Accounting

Here is where multi-provider orchestration gets interesting. You cannot use a hardcoded "5-hour rolling window" logic for everyone, because billing models vary wildly across providers:

Provider / ToolPrimary Quota MechanismDanger Threshold Factor
Codex / Antigravity5-hour rolling windows & weekly reset capsRolling utilization percentage $\ge 85%$
Claude (Anthropic)Minute-by-minute Token Bucket (RPM / TPM / TPD)Remaining daily token allowance $\le 15%$
Grok (xAI)Standard API credit burn / rate limitsRemaining prepaid account credit in USD
Copilot CLISeat-based subscription / undocumented concurrency limitsHTTP 429 Rate Limit frequency / latency spikes

To unify this for our ResourceGovernor, we replace the rigid QuotaState struct with a polymorphic Rust enum: ProviderQuota.

use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum ProviderQuota {
    RollingWindow {
        five_hour_utilization_percent: f64,
        resets_at: DateTime<Utc>,
        weekly_resets_available: u8,
    },
    TokenBucket {
        tokens_per_minute_remaining: u64,
        tokens_per_day_remaining: u64,
        resets_at: DateTime<Utc>,
    },
    CreditBurn {
        remaining_balance_usd: f64,
        auto_recharge_enabled: bool,
    },
    OpaqueSubscription {
        recent_429_count: u8,
        is_throttled: bool,
    },
}

impl ProviderQuota {
    /// Normalized health metric: Returns a value from 0.0 (Safe) to 1.0 (Critical Lockout Risk)
    pub fn calculate_throttle_risk(&self) -> f64 {
        match self {
            Self::RollingWindow { five_hour_utilization_percent, .. } => {
                five_hour_utilization_percent / 100.0
            },
            Self::TokenBucket { tokens_per_day_remaining, .. } => {
                if *tokens_per_day_remaining < 50_000 { 0.95 } else { 0.20 }
            },
            Self::CreditBurn { remaining_balance_usd, .. } => {
                if *remaining_balance_usd < 2.00 { 0.90 } else { 0.10 }
            },
            Self::OpaqueSubscription { recent_429_count, is_throttled } => {
                if *is_throttled || *recent_429_count > 3 { 1.0 } else { 0.0 }
            }
        }
    }
}

Now, your ResourceGovernor::authorize_execution() simply checks if quota.calculate_throttle_risk() >= 0.85, completely agnostic to whether the active pane is running agy, Claude, or Grok.

3. Best-of-Breed Model Routing by Role

When your system supports multiple engines natively, your clean-room multi-agent architecture gets a massive capability boost. Instead of running the same model for every persona, your orchestrator can dynamically assign different providers based on their documented strengths:

                  [Rust Roadmap Controller & State Engine]
                                     │
         ┌───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┐
         ▼                           ▼                           ▼
  [Programmer Agent]          [Tester Agent]            [Documenter Agent]
  Engine: Claude 3.5 Sonnet   Engine: Grok / agy        Engine: Codex / Copilot
  Transport: WebSockets       Transport: Stdio Pipe     Transport: Stateless Exec
  Why: Deep architectural     Why: Fast execution,      Why: Low-cost, fast file
  reasoning & coding          high-speed bug hunting    summarization & diffs

If Claude hits a rate limit midway through a milestone, the ResourceGovernor can catch the spike in calculate_throttle_risk(), transparently swap the Transport pipe over to Antigravity or Grok, and continue executing the exact same roadmap.yaml without dropping a single task.

2. The Rust Serde Domain Model (config.rs)

To parse this cleanly into strongly typed Rust structs, we use serde with internally tagged enums for the polymorphic transport configurations. This guarantees at compile time that if a profile specifies type = "WebSocket", it must also provide a valid uri string.

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::path::Path;
use tokio::fs;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq, Eq)]
#[serde(rename_all = "PascalCase")]
pub enum ProviderKind {
    Codex,
    Antigravity,
    Claude,
    Grok,
    Copilot,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "type")]
pub enum TransportConfig {
    Stdio { command: String },
    WebSocket { uri: String },

2. The In-Memory Graph Engine (petgraph)

When your Rust orchestrator boots up, it loads all .md files into a petgraph::DiGraph (a directed graph). This happens in milliseconds.

Whenever an agent modifies a note or adds a link, the orchestrator updates the in-memory graph and triggers a background Re-Gradienting Pass. The agents don't do the math; the Rust backend does.

The Re-Gradienting Math

When two graphs are merged (or a massive new cluster of notes is generated), static weights become useless. A weight of 0.8 in a 5-node graph means something entirely different in a 500-node graph.

To balance the entire graph dynamically, Rust applies an Eigenvector Centrality or PageRank-style algorithm across the network. The relative "gravity" ($G$) of any single note $i$ is recalculated based on the weights of all inbound links ($W_{ji}$) and the centrality of the nodes pointing to it ($C_j$):

$$C_i = \frac{1}{\lambda} \sum_{j \in M(i)} W_{ji} C_j$$

Where:

  • $M(i)$ is the set of notes linking to note $i$.
  • $W_{ji}$ is the agent-assigned relative weight from note $j$ to note $i$.
  • $\lambda$ is a normalization constant (the dominant eigenvalue) that ensures the entire graph's gravity sums to 1.0.

After the Rust backend calculates $C_i$ for every note, it updates an in-memory index. When an agent queries the graph (rpc:get_context_vein(topic="graphs")), the orchestrator doesn't just return matches—it sorts them by their newly balanced $C_i$ gravity score. The agent receives the most structurally important information, automatically re-weighted relative to the current state of the whole project.

Before we zoom in, let’s map out the entire topology of what we have built so far. We have constructed five distinct pillars:

1. The Execution Engine (The Clean-Room Loop)

  • Headless Transport: Moving away from fragile visual terminal scraping to robust IPC/RPC via a background app-server (using Stdio, WebSockets, or stateless Exec bursts).
  • The Orchestrator Loop: A Rust controller that manages the TMUX panes, tracks milestone completion, and automates Git commits.
  • Anti-Bloat Wipes: Forcing a branch reset and workspace wipe after every roadmap, preserving only the modular, distilled artifacts.

2. Out-of-Band State & Event Sourcing

  • The YAML Source of Truth: Moving the roadmap out of the agent’s working directory and into an encapsulated .project_state/roadmap.yaml to prevent hallucinated edits and formatting drift.
  • RPC Tool Boundaries: Agents interact with the roadmap strictly through authorized JSON-RPC functions (add_task, set_status).
  • The Immutable Ledger: Every mutation is appended to roadmap_events.log with a mandatory string justifying the change, which is then injected into the Git commit history for temporal replayability.

3. Concurrency & Preemption (The Andon Cord)

  • 1-Writer, N-Readers: A single Driver agent (Programmer) modifies the codebase, while Observer agents (Tester, Documenter) continuously read the workspace and think in the background.
  • The 1-3-5-8 Heuristic Scale: Observers evaluate architectural issues based on Complexity, Weight, and Priority.
  • Dynamic Halting: If an Observer raises a Priority 8 note, the Rust backend instantly preempts the Driver, freezing its active prompt and forcing it to resolve the critical flaw before writing another line of code.

4. Telemetry & Provider Agnosticism

  • The Resource Governor: A circuit breaker that tracks active wall-clock time, rolling token windows (e.g., 5-hour caps), and triggers conservation modes or free resets before a hard lockout occurs.
  • Polymorphic Routing: Abstracting the LLM provider so you can map different engines (Claude, Grok, local Antigravity, Copilot) to specific roles, with an automated fallback router if a model degrades or rate-limits.
  • The Canary Suite: Running a daily standardized task to catch silent model drift overnight.

5. The External Mind (Dynamic Zettelkasten)

  • Atomic Markdown Nodes: Agents externalize their chaotic "soft flow" into a decoupled metadata index of linked .md files, separating tactical chatter from code generation.
  • Live Re-Gradienting: The Rust backend loads these notes into a continuous petgraph simulation, calculating PageRank/Eigenvector centrality to automatically balance link weights and surface the most structurally critical "veins" of thought.
  • Artifact Compression: At the end of a milestone, the heavy, sprawling graph is distilled into a single, dense ARCHITECTURE.md file, and the raw notes are archived to keep the next iteration lean.
